Messages.Author: Blooded Sand
Messages.Body:
If a player was to put numbers, from 1-90, on the play side of his
cards, inside the sleeve, which he would use to "reset" his deck,
before shuffling, would that qualify as marking cards or stacking his
deck?

Messages.Author: Ankur Gupta
Messages.Body:
> If a player was to put numbers, from 1-90, on the play side of his
> cards, inside the sleeve, which he would use to "reset" his deck, before
> shuffling, would that qualify as marking cards or stacking his deck?

I don't know about marking cards, but assuming that your shuffling process
is sufficiently randomized (i.e. 20 or more shuffles), it should not
matter at all which order the cards were in prior to beginning the
shuffling process. In fact, if such a stacking were to create "better
shuffles" for the player in question, then it's almost certainly not being
sufficiently randomized.

Bottom line: Randomize your deck sufficiently, and initial ordering does
not matter. If it does matter, you're not random.

Ankur Gupta
Prince of West Lafayette

> to let anyone else shuffle if they felt like it. Eventually he said
> that seeing as each time he has to figure out in his head what order
> they need to be put in before they are shuffled top ensure an even
> spread of card types,

There's the problem. If being shuffled "quite well" is well enough to
meet the "sufficiently" requirement of the VEKN rules, then the cards
don't "need" to be in any particular order, sub-order, partial-order,
or spread.

That is, the final arrangement (clumping, spread, and all) of the deck
is independent of whatever the original order is if the deck is being
shuffled "sufficiently".

If the starting arrangement is having a noticeable (and intentional)
effect on the final arrangement, then the V:EKN rules on sufficient
randomization are being violated.

The thing is, however, that something like a 'perfect shuffle' does not
exists. If I put all my cards sorted by what card it is (like, when you
first construct it) and then shuffle it 'sufficiently' for like 20 times, I
end up with a crappy spread of cards. Like stacks of 4-5 masters in a row
etc simply because of the starting position of the cards. One might argue
that I haven't shuffled properly, but nobody shuffles his deck 70-80 times
because it's inconvenient and time-consuming. Hence, in any given game, the
cards are not entirely randomized; they're randomized based on what order
they were in before you started shuffling.

That said, the starting position of the cards DO have influence on the order
they end up and putting your cards evenly spread through the deck is
blatantly cheating IMO; even if done without markers. If I out all my 5-card
combo's together in stacks of 5 before shuffling, those same combo's are
very likely to end up close together even after shuffling 'sufficiently'
simply because in practice the shuffing is far from sufficient to actually
randomize the deck. This is also why you see players lay out the cards in 6
or 7 stacks between games before shuffling instead of shuffling right away.

Part of the problem is that "sufficiently randomized" isn't
well-defined. In practice, people evaluate the randomizing algorithms
subjectively --- out of necessity, since the correct definition of
randomizing algorithm involves it passing several statistical tests. But

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Izaak wrote:
> The thing is, however, that something like a 'perfect shuffle' does not
> exists. If I put all my cards sorted by what card it is (like, when you
> first construct it) and then shuffle it 'sufficiently' for like 20 times, I
> end up with a crappy spread of cards. Like stacks of 4-5 masters in a row
> etc simply because of the starting position of the cards.

If you shuffle 20 times and a group of 5 cards has managed to stick
together through each of those 20 shuffles, then the cards or sleeves
are faulty (sticky) or the shuffling method for your individual shuffle
needs to be examined to find the flaw and remove it.

If you just overhand the deck a few times (equivalent to six to ten
stacks that are then reversed in there ordering), then, yes, 20
shuffles is not sufficient.

If, however, you're doing a reasonable riffle shuffle or pile shuffle,
then 20 would certainly be sufficient.

That said, you can expect some clumping in a "random" arrangement of
cards. If you can validly expect little to no clumping, then your
shuffling isn't random.

> One might argue
> that I haven't shuffled properly, but nobody shuffles his deck 70-80 times
> because it's inconvenient and time-consuming. Hence, in any given game, the
> cards are not entirely randomized; they're randomized based on what order
> they were in before you started shuffling.

No matter how well shuffled, the cards are never technically entirely
randomized. The point is that they be sufficiently randomized --
meaning any pre existing arrangement of the cards has no predictable
effect on the final arrangement of cards.

> That said, the starting position of the cards DO have influence on the order
> they end up and putting your cards evenly spread through the deck is
> blatantly cheating IMO; even if done without markers. If I out all my 5-card
> combo's together in stacks of 5 before shuffling, those same combo's are
> very likely to end up close together even after shuffling 'sufficiently'
> simply because in practice the shuffing is far from sufficient to actually
> randomize the deck.

Not true. If you shuffle sufficiently, then those combos are no more
likely to be together than any other set of 5 cards are.

> This is also why you see players lay out the cards in 6
> or 7 stacks between games before shuffling instead of shuffling right away.

Pile shuffling *is* shuffling (assuming it's done with the cards face
down).

> and start playing.
>

Of course.

Pile shuffling should be done as "randomly" as possible. Stacking a
deck so that a methodical pile shuffle will move certain cards together
is not a shuffle at all.

And even so, a real pile shufle should be followed by real riffle
shuffles, not loose ones. Preferably alternating between them (real
pile shuffles and real riffle shuffles).

For more on this topic, see
http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/1d7d6d2ab6808242
and surrounding posts.

In any event, if you hand a deck to your predator to cut when you know
the deck is not sufficiently randomized (regardless of the motions you
may have put the cards through, and especially if you put them through
motions desined to effect a particular outcome, clumping, spread,
etc.), then you are, by definition, cheating.

randomization doesn't answer the question of what IS a randomization
method. How are judges to determine when a deck is sufficiently
randomized? The OP wrote that he thought the shuffling was proper, and
that the player offered the deck up for others to shuffle. If it was
sufficiently randomized (by objective criteria) then there is no problem
with numbering the faces. If it wasn't randomized, then not only is the

inability to determine whether or not a deck has been randomized. That
is my whole point.

In order to know what "randomization" is, look at the _point_ of what you're
doing. The point of shuffling your deck before a game is so that you won't
know anything about what order the cards will appear in. If you have some
knowledge (or if others at the table have some knowledge) (and it isn't
based on illegal marking, of course) of what cards are going to come up in
which order, then your deck isn't randomized. Of course, this includes
knowledge based on what cards have appeared previously and it also includes
mere suspicions or non-equal likelyhoods. So, if you've drawn a master
card and you're thinking this indicates the likely of another master card
appearing immediately behind it, something's wrong with your randomization.
If you've drawn a master card and you feel fairly confident that it will
_not_ be followed by another master card (that is, more confident than
you should given the odds of the remaining number of master cards divided
by the remaining number of cards in the deck), then something's wrong with
your randomization.

All of these points seem quite obvious to me. I'm wondering what your
actual issue is here. I don't really understand what the thrust of your
question is.

> The OP wrote that he thought the shuffling was proper, and
> that the player offered the deck up for others to shuffle.

Sure. But that was, of course, incredibly illogical. If his shuffling
was "proper", then he should not have needed any order printed on his
cards to put them in so that he would feel them any more or less
"randomized" when he got done shuffling. Either his perception was
flawed or his method of shuffling was. There's no third option. And
offering the deck to others to shuffle is beside the point. Others
shouldn't need to shuffle his deck in order to assure that they're
randomized. If they do, he's cheating.

> If it was
> sufficiently randomized (by objective criteria) then there is no problem
> with numbering the faces.

Agreed. It's simply an illogical, unnecessary act - by definition.

> If it wasn't randomized, then not only is the
> player's shuffling algorithm flawed, but the judge has demonstrated his
> inability to determine whether or not a deck has been randomized. That
> is my whole point.

Sure. Judges are limited in their ability to have total knowledge of
whether a deck is truly randomized or not - but they have to make rulings
about it anyway. There are many issues judges have to rule on without
the ability or knowledge to make a flawless ruling. I fail to see what
point you're making beyond this. We already knew this.

Fred

Yes, of course. That's not the issue at hand IMO. By allowing pre-stacking
of a deck you're also taking a very big assumption that every deck is
completely randomized before starting a game. That in itself is simply not
the case. Another example:

I play a deck with 25 Thefts of Vitae, 25 Apportations, 20 Conditionings and
20 permanents. Naturally, after the first round, my ashpile will consist
only the Thefts, Apportations and Conditiongs. I gather my cards from the
table, add them to the ashpile and reshuffle the for the next round. Not too
surprisingly, the next round most of the permanents will be close together
in the deck, even though I didn't even try to accomplish that and shuffled
'sufficiently'

Incidentally, exactly this is also what causes people to master jam a lot on
second and third rounds, but that ofc might be just my experience in recent
tournaments. I personally always make a point of it to make sure my masters
are spread fairly well through the deck before starting to shuffle it to
decrease the chance of them being clumped together when I'm done shuffling.
In a way, this might be considered cheating too now that I think of it...

> My question is: How does one practically determine if a deck has been

> predict which cards are going to be drawn next is irrelevant, because

By shuffling well and often. It's the only way. Riffle Shuffle several
times. Pile Shuffle, then Riffle Shuffle the piles together. Then Poker
Shuffle a little. Then Riffle Shuffle several more times. Then Pile
Shuffle again. Then Riffle Shuffle the piles together. Then Poker
Shuffle a little...

sufficiently randomize a 90-card deck. Most people shuffle 2-4 times
and call it a day.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <5BxXf.7406$4L1....@newssvr11.news.prodigy.com>, Brett

<shugNOo...@sbcglobal.net> writes:
>I don't dispute that. But demonstrating one method that does not
>produce randomization doesn't answer the question of what IS a
>randomization method. How are judges to determine when a deck is
>sufficiently randomized?

By using their judgement. While any number of guidelines can be given,
it essentially boils down to that.

If a judge has any reason to believe that a given deck has been
insufficiently shuffled, they can just pick up the deck, shuffle it and
award a table extra time if necessary. Though if the table lacks any
"Look at the top three cards" sort of effects, the judge could just
continue shuffling while play continues, and hand the player a card
whenever he needs to draw. That is aside from any judgements on whether
the infraction was intentional or not.

If you're particularly worried about this, hand each table a die with a
reasonable number of faces on it - perhaps 6 to 10. Get each player to
roll the die, add a small number to it (say, 2) and then get their
predator to pile shuffle into d6+2 piles. Repeat as necessary until
everyone thoroughly shuffles their decks in front of the other players
anyway.

For the players who are particularly worried about their preciouses
being touched by other people, tell them to bring sleeves or get a/the
judge to do it. A judge is going to need the authority to go through
their deck in some circumstances anyway, such as if the judge is trying
to satisfy himself that a given deal is play-to-win because the player
protests that he's trying strategy X, or if a player alleges that
certain cards have been discarded to the top of the library, or
whatever.

In any event, many players will often ask to have a look through an ash
heap. And pile shuffling is probably the best form of randomization
that doesn't involve people with no co-ordination (such as me) trying
to riffle shuffle.

Messages.Author: LSJ

Izaak wrote:
> > Of course.
> Then pre-stacking would be cheating.

Not in-and-of itself, no.
On top of the underlying infraction (failure to sufficiently randomize
the deck), it could be cause to increase the penalty for the
infraction, though.

> > Pile shuffling should be done as "randomly" as possible. Stacking a
> > deck so that a methodical pile shuffle will move certain cards together
> > is not a shuffle at all.
>
> Okay, so I "randomly" pile shuffle. Ie, I put my 90 cards in a certain order
> and then pile shuffle them seemingly random, while in fact it is a
> pre-determined pattern putting my cards in the optimal playing order.

The "i.e.," above is not appropriate. "i.e." means that the thing that
follows is equivalent to the thing that went before. But "randomly" is
clearly not equivalent to "causing to become arranged in a
pre-determined pattern". Indeed, they are complete antonyms.

> Sure,
> I'm cheating, but it's an undetectable way to cheat if pre-stacking cards in
> a certain order is allowed.

Non-sequitur.
The discussion is about what is cheating, not about how to detect
cheating.

You are cheating, as you say. QED.

> > And even so, a real pile shufle should be followed by real riffle
> > shuffles, not loose ones. Preferably alternating between them (real
> > pile shuffles and real riffle shuffles).
>
> With a loose shuffle I mean a 2-3 riffle shuffles using fairly big clumps of
> cards with each motion. Dunno if that makes sense, but it's how people tend
> to shuffle cards in tournaments.

If you mean some method that fails to sufficiently randomize the decks,
then the people who tend to use that method need to be instructed to
use some other method so as to conform to the rules.

> > For more on this topic, see
> > http://groups.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/1d7d6d2ab6808242
> > and surrounding posts.
> >
> > In any event, if you hand a deck to your predator to cut when you know
> > the deck is not sufficiently randomized (regardless of the motions you
> > may have put the cards through, and especially if you put them through
> > motions desined to effect a particular outcome, clumping, spread,
> > etc.), then you are, by definition, cheating.
>
> Yes, of course. That's not the issue at hand IMO.

?
It is exactly and directly the issue -- the quote above is a direct
response to that exact issue.

> By allowing pre-stacking
> of a deck you're also taking a very big assumption that every deck is
> completely randomized before starting a game. That in itself is simply not
> the case.

A deck is always pre-stacked prior to shuffling. Of course it is
allowed -- it cannot be disallowed.

In other news, taking that stack and taking time to manipulate the
arrangement into some other arrangement (looking at the faces -- not
shuffling), while allowed, is pointless if the subsequent shuffling
process generates a sufficient randomization. So manipulating the deck
prior to shuffling is a signal to everyone that the shuffling that will
follow should be carefully scrutinized for signs insufficient
randomization.

> Another example:
>
> I play a deck with 25 Thefts of Vitae, 25 Apportations, 20 Conditionings and
> 20 permanents. Naturally, after the first round, my ashpile will consist
> only the Thefts, Apportations and Conditiongs. I gather my cards from the
> table, add them to the ashpile and reshuffle the for the next round. Not too
> surprisingly, the next round most of the permanents will be close together
> in the deck, even though I didn't even try to accomplish that and shuffled
> 'sufficiently'

Then your shuffle is insufficiently random if it allows this sort of
predictable outcome based on the starting stacking of the deck.

> Incidentally, exactly this is also what causes people to master jam a lot on
> second and third rounds, but that ofc might be just my experience in recent
> tournaments. I personally always make a point of it to make sure my masters
> are spread fairly well through the deck before starting to shuffle it to
> decrease the chance of them being clumped together when I'm done shuffling.
> In a way, this might be considered cheating too now that I think of it...

Yes, indeed.

Messages.Author: LSJ

Izaak wrote:
> So in short: if I stack my cards in whatever way I like, even using numbers
> to do so. and then rifle shuffle it 9 times, as suggested a 90-card deck
> takes to be 'sufficiently shuffled' I'm ok?

If your 9 riffle shuffles sufficiently randomize the deck, then you're
OK.
If your 9 riffle shuffles fail to sufficiently randomize the deck
(e.g., they're "perfect" riffles, or they're less-than-adquate
riffles), then you're not OK.

In short: it does't matter what method you use, so long as you
sufficiently randomize your deck.

> If I saw a player at my table do that I'd call a judge. If you were that
> judge what would you do? Allow it?

I'd make sure the player sufficiently randomizes his deck. And I'd
explain the fruitlessness of pre-stacking to the player while I was at
it.

Let him order it.

Then take the deck off him, and order it into a fashion that would be
bad if the deck wasn't thoroughly randomized first, such as putting all
the Blood Dolls together at the bottom, or no combat in the top fifty
cards, or alphabetised in a fashion of your choice, or with all the key

> If a player was to put numbers, from 1-90, on the play side of his

It should make no difference, as has been stated ad infinitem. In fact
7 riffle shuffles are sufficient to fully randomize a 52 card deck (see
http://www.sciencenews.org/articles/20001014/mathtrek.asp, not sure if
a 90 card deck would need more or less shuffles my guess would be
less). Casinos, where time shuffling is wasted time as no one can bet,
often settle on 5 or 6. This however, is with a decent shuffler using
the riffle technique. There is an added problem, card sleeves. These
prevent a deck being shuffled successfully as the increased friction
between cards and the increased thickness of each card prevents a clean
shuffle.
If I were in your position I would not allow the the guy to number his
cards if he uses sleeves. If he wants to foresake his sleves and write
on the front of each of his cards with a magic marker ... then that's
fine.

No. Your deck is sufficiently shuffled when your predator and the
tournament judge are both satisfied that it is. When you present your
deck to your predator, he may not only cut it, but shuffle it until he
is satisfied it has been randomized. Then the judge has complete
authority to decide if it has been randomized, and order further
shuffling. There is no hard rule about what constitutes "sufficiently
shuffled".

extra shuffling simply to ensure the player was receiving no
statistical benefits.
